about: B73: one faithful hand-written text per record (PRE-17), written before the checker existed. The checker should pass all of them (decision rule: at least 9 of 10).

texts.text: In the early winter of year 37, at Harum, the winter camp of the Kesh band, Imra, a woman of 19, was shaping a scraper. She struck cutting stone against a lump of heavy yellow stone, and sparks fell on the dry moss beside her. The moss began to smoke. Imra blew on it, and it caught fire. Her brother Tavu saw it. She tried 3 more times that day, and twice more the moss caught fire. Until then, the Kesh band had kept fire only by carrying embers from camp to camp. No one in the world had made fire by striking stones before. Imra was unsure, but she believed that fire lives inside the yellow stone.

Hear this, and remember Oru. Oru of the Kesh band broke his leg in a fall in autumn. After that he could not walk far. In deep winter the food ran out at Harum, the cold hollow. So the band moved to Ulmeke, the red cliff, 4 days' walk away. The band left Oru behind at Harum. They left him a small fire and 2 strips of dried meat. His daughter Sefi was the last to leave him. On his fourth night alone the fire went out, and Oru died of the cold. 10 days later, 2 hunters found his body beside the dead fire.

In the spring of year 52, at night, in the Tulo camp on the shore of Sefa, the wide water, Kaya gave birth to a girl. Kaya was 22. Her mother Anwe, 44, and Lisu, 30, helped her through a labour that lasted most of the night. The girl was small, and she cried at once. She is Kaya's second child; the first, a boy, is 3 years old. The girl has no name yet: the Tulo band believes a child is given a name only after it lives through its first winter.

Listen. This is how Moro died. It was late summer, at dusk. Anuk of the Kesh band waited for Moro at Teshu, the shallow crossing. When Moro came to cross, Anuk killed him. He drove his spear, with its cutting stone point, into Moro's belly. Moro died at the ford before dark. His sister Ishe saw it from the far bank. Ishe ran to our camp and told us. Anuk was sure Moro had killed his brother Pell in the spring. That is why Anuk killed Moro.

In the autumn of year 70, the Amaru band, 26 people, argued for 2 days at Ulmeke, the red cliff, over where to spend the winter. Hesh, 40, wanted to go to Kotara, the salt shore, 6 days' walk away; he was sure the shellfish there do not run out in winter. Nima, 46, wanted to stay at Ulmeke, among its dry caves; she was sure the walk was too long for the old and for small children. The band split. 11 people went with Hesh to Kotara, and 15 stayed with Nima. Rafi, the son of Hesh, stayed with Nima.

Hear the dream of Dabo. In late winter the lake Sefa was frozen over. Dabo meant to cross the ice to hunt on the far shore, for crossing the ice saves a day of walking. He was sure the ice was strong enough. But that night he dreamt of his dead mother, Ama. She stood on the ice, and the ice broke under her. When Dabo woke, he was no longer sure. He thought the ice might break. So he did not cross. He walked around the lake, and it took him 2 days. That same morning Pek and Hanu crossed the ice, and they came back safe.

In the winter of year 118, at night, at Harum, the woman Shana, 51, told the story Tara-mi, "the coming of fire", to 14 listeners. Imra first told it in year 45. In her telling, fire lived inside the heavy yellow stone, and a woman named Imra struck the stone, and fire jumped into the moss. In Shana's telling, the sky put fire inside the heavy yellow stone, and the first mother struck the stone, and fire jumped into the dry grass. The sky had been added, the name Imra had been lost, and the moss had become dry grass.

Listen. In summer, in a storm, sky-fire struck the lone tall tree on the ridge above our camp at Ulmeke. The tree split. The tree burned. No one was hurt. Then Nima spoke. She said the sky-fire was a sign: the dead no longer wanted us at Ulmeke. Nima was sure. 17 of us 20 came to believe her, though we were not sure. 3 days later we left Ulmeke, the red cliff, and walked toward Sefa, the wide water.

In late autumn of year 95, before dawn, 7 men of the Kesh band, led by Kelo, 33, attacked the Tulo camp on the shore of Sefa. The Kesh band had killed little game that autumn, and Kelo was sure the Tulo camp had more dried meat than it needed. The raiders killed Gudo, 38, with clubs. They took Rena, 17, and Oshi, 15, captive, tied their hands with sinew cord, and made them carry the Tulo band's dried meat to the Kesh camp. The other Tulo people fled into the reeds.

Hear how we met the Amaru band. It was spring, at midday, at Teshu, the shallow crossing. We met them by chance. We had no words in common, so we pointed, and we laid things on the ground. Temo gave 3 lumps of red earth to Yari of the Amaru. Yari gave Temo a string of 12 white shells from Kotara, the salt shore. The two bands camped apart for 1 night. The next morning we went our separate ways.
